options.A: Beautiful furniture make the house elegant and looks sophisticated at the same time.
options.B: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is thousands of years old and has changed little over the centuries.
options.C: Folktales can be used to help children develop strong reading skills, study other cultures, and discover a love of stories.
options.D: Clothing is expensive because of the financial shakeup it received during the COVID-19 pandemic.
options.a: Beautiful furniture make the house elegant and looks sophisticated at the same time.
options.b: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is thousands of years old and has changed little over the centuries.
options.c: Folktales can be used to help children develop strong reading skills, study other cultures, and discover a love of stories.
options.d: Clothing is expensive because of the financial shakeup it received during the COVID-19 pandemic.

solution:
The incorrect sentence is "Beautiful furniture make the house elegant and looks sophisticated at the same time."

Rule: Furniture is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: makes. The two actions must also be parallel.
Correct sentence: Beautiful furniture makes the house elegant and sophisticated at the same time.

The other three sentences are grammatically correct.
conceptTested: Uncountable nouns (like furniture) are treated as singular and take singular verbs.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts, namely A, B, C and D, which are given in the alternatives. Select the alternative that contains the part of the sentence with an error.

The ancient ruins attract thousands of tourists every year who are fascinating by the rich history and culture of the place.

options.B: of tourists every year who are
options.b: of tourists every year who are

solution:
The error is in part C: fascinating by should be fascinated by.
Rule: The past participle (fascinated) describes how a person feels; the - ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Correct sentence: The ancient ruins attract thousands of tourists every year who are fascinated by the rich history and culture of the place.
conceptTested: Past participles (-ed form) are used to describe feelings, whereas present participles (-ing form) describe the source or cause of the feeling.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
The sentence below has errors in two parts which are highlighted in bold. Identify the same.

The reef is on risk of (A) losing its coveted World Heritage Status on occasion of (B) ocean warming, fuelled by (C) climate change, which is damaging its health(D).
solution:
The errors are in parts A and B.

A: "on risk of" $\rightarrow$ at risk of (fixed phrase meaning "in danger of").
B: "on occasion of" $\rightarrow$ on account of / because of; a cause is needed here, while "on the occasion of" means "at the time of an event".
Correct sentence: The reef is at risk of losing its coveted World Heritage Status on account of ocean warming, fuelled by climate change, which is damaging its health.

Parts C and D are correct, so the answer is BA.
conceptTested: Fixed prepositional phrases such as 'at risk of' and causal prepositions like 'on account of' must be used correctly.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the error in the below-given sentence.

"The police has arrested the suspect in the case".
solution:
The error is "has".

Rule: Police is a collective noun always used in the plural, so it takes have. (Similarly: cattle, people, clergy.)
Correct sentence: The police have arrested the suspect in the case.
conceptTested: Plural collective nouns (such as police, cattle, people) always take plural verbs.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the grammatical error in the sentence below.

The news that the plane had crashed will be coming as a terrible shock.
solution:
The error lies in part 3: will be coming.
Rule & Explanation: The future continuous tense ('will be coming') expresses an action in progress at a specific time in the future. However, receiving news and experiencing emotional shock occurs as a punctual event, not a continuous process. When stating the predictable effect of dramatic news, English uses the simple future: 'will come as a terrible shock' (or 'came as a terrible shock').
Correct sentence: The news that the plane had crashed will come as a terrible shock.
conceptTested: Punctual events or inevitable outcomes use simple future tense rather than future continuous tense.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the grammatical error in the sentence below.

The bank will be continued to transfer the interest to your account unless instructed otherwise.
solution:
The error lies in part 2: will be continued.
Rule & Explanation: The subject 'The bank' is the active agent performing the action of transferring interest, not the recipient of the action. The passive construction 'will be continued to transfer' is grammatically incorrect. The verb must be in the active voice: 'will continue to transfer'.
Correct sentence: The bank will continue to transfer the interest to your account unless instructed otherwise.
conceptTested: Subject-verb agreement and voice: Subjects performing an action require active voice constructions rather than incorrect passive forms.

subject: English Comprehension

options.A: She has got cold and cough.
options.B: Only a few people came to the party.
options.C: Could you lend me some of your books today?
options.D: He has more sense than you have.
options.a: She has got cold and cough.
options.b: Only a few people came to the party.
options.c: Could you lend me some of your books today?
options.d: He has more sense than you have.

solution:
The incorrect sentence is Option 1.

Rule & Explanation: In standard English idiom, the illnesses 'cold' and 'cough' are singular countable nouns that require indefinite articles: one catches or suffers from 'a cold' and 'a cough'. Thus, the correct idiomatic expression is 'She has got a cold and a cough'.
• Option 2 correctly uses 'a few' with countable 'people'.
• Option 3 correctly uses 'some' in a polite request expected to elicit an affirmative response.
• Option 4 correctly uses the comparative 'more sense than'.
conceptTested: Usage of indefinite articles with singular countable idiomatic illnesses like 'a cold' and 'a cough'.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts, namely A, B, C and D, which are given in the alternatives. Select the alternative that contains the part of the sentence with an error.

Remember to brush your teeth thorough before you go to bed every single night without fail as instructed by the dentist.

options.B: thorough before you go to bed
options.b: thorough before you go to bed

solution:
Error: "brush" is a verb, so it must be modified by an adverb. “Thorough” is an adjective; the adverb is “thoroughly”.
Correct: Remember to brush your teeth thoroughly before you go to bed ...

The other parts are correct.

Therefore, thorough before you go to bed.
conceptTested: Adverbs modify verbs, whereas adjectives modify nouns. Verbs of action like 'brush' must be modified by adverbs ('thoroughly').

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

In Woolf's imaginary legacy (1)/, the room functions not just as sanctuary (2)/ but also as a discursive axis (3)/ where womanhood collapse into multiplicity. (4)
solution:
Rule: The subject womanhood is an uncountable singular noun and requires a singular verb (collapses) in the present simple tense.
Correction: "...where womanhood collapses into multiplicity."

Parts (1), (2), and (3) are grammatically sound.
conceptTested: Subject-Verb Agreement: Uncountable singular nouns (e.g., womanhood) require singular present tense verb forms (collapses).

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

Despite its ostensible neutrality (1)/, the bureaucratic apparatus (2)/ enact normative controls (3)/ that homogenize diverse expressions of identity. (4)
solution:
Rule: The subject apparatus is singular in this context and requires the singular present verb form enacts.
Correction: "...the bureaucratic apparatus enacts normative controls..."

The remaining clauses are constructed correctly.
conceptTested: Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular collective or common nouns (e.g., apparatus) require singular verb forms in the present tense (enacts).

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

The researcher who the panel had nominated (1)/ for the ethics award (2)/ were present at the plenary session (3)/ but declined to speak. (4)
solution:
Rule: The head subject of the sentence is the singular noun 'The researcher', which demands the singular past verb 'was' rather than the plural 'were'.
Correction: "...was present at the plenary session..."

Parts (1), (2), and (4) are grammatically correct.
conceptTested: Subject-Verb Agreement: The verb must agree in number with its true head subject ('The researcher'), requiring the singular verb 'was' instead of the plural 'were'.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

The researchers insisted (1)/ on replacing the control group (2)/ by another cohort (3)/ with matched characteristics. (4)
solution:
Rule: The standard collocation for replacing one entity with an alternative is replace X with Y (not *replace by*).
Correction: "...with another cohort..."

Parts (1), (2), and (4) correctly handle standard verbs and phrases.
conceptTested: Fixed Prepositions / Collocations: The correct preposition used with the verb 'replace' in this context is 'with' (replace X with Y), not 'by'.

subject: English Comprehension
questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

You must to ensure that (1)/ all parameters are recorded (2)/ before the simulation (3)/ can be rerun. (4)
solution:
Rule: Modal auxiliary verbs such as must are followed directly by a bare infinitive without the particle *to* (i.e., 'must ensure').
Correction: "You must ensure that..."

Parts (2), (3), and (4) are grammatically correct.
conceptTested: Use of Modal Auxiliaries: Modal verbs like 'must' are followed directly by a bare infinitive without the particle 'to'.
